title: Know what you sing
hook: a ragged man walks into a king's sacrifice and stops the singers cold: do you know what you're singing to?
carry: the sama veda: sacred song, sung knowing what it means

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer at the river. Svasti: ask all the gods to keep us well.

A king holds a great sacrifice, and his singers take their places. Into the hall walks a ragged man. Not long before, in a famine, he was eating a stranger's leftover beans. Now he sits down beside the king's chanters, and as they begin, he turns to each one: if you sing this without knowing the god it belongs to, your head will fall off. The singing stops. His name is Ushasti, and the songs are the Sama Veda's. Today: the Veda as song.
screen: `A RAGGED MAN AT THE KING'S RITE.` → `"DO YOU KNOW WHAT YOU'RE SINGING TO?"` → `THE VEDA AS SONG.`

segments.voice: The Sama Veda is the Veda of melodies. Saman means a chant, and its verses are ones that also appear in the Rig Veda, gathered and set to tune for the singers of the rite. It even opens with a call to the fire: agna a yahi vitaye, come, Agni, to the feast. In the great rites some priests recited and others sang, led by the udgatri, the chief singer. Those are the singers Ushasti stops, in the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda. The king, alarmed, asks who he is, and hires him on the spot. Then the singers ask: so what are the gods of our chants? He tells them. The opening chant belongs to breath, because every creature enters and leaves life with breath. The high chant belongs to the sun, because every creature sings to it when it rises high. The response belongs to food, because every creature lives by taking it in. Breath, sun, food: what keeps you alive is what you're singing to. Near its start the same Upanishad puts the teaching in one line: what is done with knowledge, with faith, and with its inner meaning becomes stronger. That's why Hindu tradition prizes melody and meaning together. The tune carries the words in; knowing what they mean lets you sing them on purpose. A bhajan, an aarti, a mantra at a havan: sung knowing what it says, it is more than sound.
screen: `SAMAN: A CHANT, A MELODY.` · `"DO YOU KNOW THE GOD OF YOUR CHANT?"` · `BREATH. THE SUN. FOOD.` · `KNOWLEDGE AND FAITH MAKE IT STRONGER.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you know by heart: an aarti, a bhajan, a mantra, or simply Om. Before you sing it, think for a moment about what it means; if you aren't sure, hold the one word you do know. Then sing or hum it once, slowly, meaning it; if you can't make sound where you are, say it silently. If you don't pray, use a line from a song that matters to you.
The Sama Veda as song. Saman, melody: Rig Veda verses set to tune and, as Ushasti taught the king's singers, sung knowing what they're for. Today's word.

howItsDone: The Sama Veda is learned from a teacher by ear, melody and all, and in the Vedic rites its chants belong to the priests who sing; at home, many families sing aarti and bhajans, often in the evening.

options: the Chandogya says what's done with knowledge and faith is stronger. learn what it says, then sing it for nani.

chat.meaning: Ushasti stopped the king's singers for chanting without knowing what each chant was for, and the Chandogya teaches that what's done with knowledge, faith and inner meaning is stronger. Melody and meaning go together.
